finding: §3.3 pins write-time validation of an invalid review_converge_on only for the task-layer command `tp set --workflow review_converge_on=<bad>` (exit 2, usage), and Test 17 (§11.17) tests only that path. The sanctioned way to populate the project layer is `tp set --workflow --project review_converge_on=<value>` (writes .tp/config.json) — also a command-line argument. The spec never states whether that project-layer set validates the literal at write time (exit 2, like the task-layer set) or persists the bad value silently so it only fails later at exit 1 under the 'invalid winning value from a stored layer (.tp/config.json)' clause. Both readings are consistent with the text, so a QA engineer cannot write a deterministic exit-code test for `tp set --workflow --project review_converge_on=bad`.
suggestion: State in §3.3 that BOTH `tp set --workflow` and `tp set --workflow --project` validate the literal argument at write time and reject with exit 2 (so no bad value is ever persisted through the sanctioned commands, and the exit-1 stored-layer case is reserved for hand-edited files), and add the --project write path to Test 17.

finding: §5.2 defines the over-specification class as 'a detail whose correctness can only be established against code' — phrasing that reads as mechanizable, since a gate check registered via `checks`/`mechanize_candidates` is precisely 'establishing correctness against code'. But §8.2 excludes over-specification from the mechanize_candidates branch because it is 'un-mechanizable by definition — no gate check can verify an altitude smell (§5.2, §10.3)'. The two sections invoke the same 'against code' property to draw opposite conclusions (checkable-against-code vs. un-mechanizable), and the reconciling distinction — the over-specified detail is code-checkable once moved into task acceptance, whereas the altitude judgment 'this is over-specified' is not itself a gate check — is never stated at the point of collision, so §5.2 and §8.2 read as contradictory on whether over-specification is mechanizable.
suggestion: Make the distinction explicit at one of the two sites: in §5.2 clarify that the *detail's* correctness is establishable against code once it lives in task acceptance (where the gate runs), while the *finding* that a detail is over-specified is an altitude judgment, not a runnable check; then §8.2's 'un-mechanizable' exclusion refers unambiguously to the finding/judgment, not to the underlying detail.
